slides.title: Little marks, big jobs
slides.text:
Some marks look like small lines or dots.

A **hyphen** ( - ) is short. A **dash** ( — ) is long. An **ellipsis** ( ... ) is three dots.

slides.title: The hyphen joins
slides.text:
A hyphen **joins words** so they work as one.

**twenty-one**  **ice-cold**  **a six-year-old boy**

slides.title: Dots make you wait
slides.text:
An ellipsis ( ... ) shows a **pause**.

The reader slows down and waits.

The box opened... and out came a kitten!

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
Look at the words **next to** the mark.

1. Find the hyphen, dash or dots.
2. Ask: does it **join** words or make a **pause**?
3. Point to the sentence that shows it.

example.explain: **seven-year-old** has two hyphens. They join three words into one describing word for the sister.

together.passage: My brother got a red bike today. He rode it twenty one times around the yard. Then he sat down on the grass.
together.hint: Look for a number made of two words. Numbers from 21 to 99 use a hyphen.
together.good: Yes! It should be **twenty-one**. The hyphen joins the two number words.

sentences: My brother got a red bike today.
He rode it twenty one times around the yard.
Then he sat down on the grass.
evidence.stem: The answer was: twenty one needs a hyphen. Tap the sentence with those words.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no words that need joining. Find the sentence with a number.

checks.passage: It was a very hot day. Mom made ice cold juice. We drank it in the shade.
checks.why: **ice-cold** joins two words to make one describing word for the juice.

checks.passage: Sara opened the box slowly. Inside was... a tiny kitten!
checks.stem: Why does the writer use the dots ( ... )?
checks.why: The dots make a pause, so the reader waits to find out what is in the box.

checks.passage: Our class has thirty two students. Each student has a desk.
checks.stem: How should the number be written?
checks.why: Two-word numbers from 21 to 99 use a short hyphen: **thirty-two**.

again.title: Join or wait?
again.text:
Ask one question about the mark.

1. Is it **short** and between two words? It **joins** them.
2. Is it **three dots**? It makes you **wait**.
again.example:
We ate forty-two dates.  → the hyphen joins **forty** and **two**.

I think... yes!  → the dots make a pause.

slides.title: Three marks
slides.text:
1. **Hyphen** ( - ): joins words into one idea.
2. **Dash** ( — ): adds a strong break or extra information.
3. **Ellipsis** ( ... ): shows a pause or words that trail off.

slides.title: Hyphens before a noun
slides.text:
When two words describe a noun **together**, join them with a hyphen.

a **well-known** museum
a **two-hour** trip
a **sugar-free** drink

slides.title: Dash and ellipsis
slides.text:
A dash makes the reader **notice** what comes next.

The winner was — Huda!

An ellipsis shows someone **stopping** or **thinking**.

"I left my bag at..." Noor stopped.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To prove what a mark does:

1. Find the mark in the text.
2. Read the words **before and after** it.
3. Ask: is it joining words, giving a strong break, or showing a pause?

The sentence with the mark is your proof.

sentences.t: We went on a two-hour boat trip.
We saw dolphins near the coast.

example.explain: **two** and **hour** describe the trip together, so a hyphen joins them: **two-hour** trip.

together.passage: Khalid had trained for weeks. On the day of the race, the sun was burning. He passed one runner, then another. At the finish line he saw someone he did not expect — his grandfather, cheering louder than anyone. Khalid smiled all the way home.
together.stem: Why does the writer use a dash ( — ) in the text?
together.hint: Find the dash. What comes right after it? Is it something Khalid expected?
together.good: Yes! The dash makes us stop for a moment before the surprise: his grandfather.

sentences: On the day of the race, the sun was burning.
He passed one runner, then another.
At the finish line he saw someone he did not expect — his grandfather, cheering louder than anyone.
Khalid smiled all the way home.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the dash sets up a surprise. Tap the sentence with the dash.
evidence.wrong: This sentence has no dash. Find the sentence where the dash comes before the surprise.

checks.passage: Last week we visited a well known museum in Riyadh. We saw old coins and maps.
checks.why: **well** and **known** describe the museum together, so they need a hyphen: a **well-known** museum.

checks.passage: "I think I left my lunch at..." Noor stopped. She was not sure where she had left it.
options: Noor stops before she finishes speaking.
checks.why: The dots show Noor's words trail off. The next sentences say she stopped and was not sure.

checks.passage: The oldest tree in our garden — a sidr tree — gives shade all summer.
checks.stem: What do the two dashes do?
options: They show a pause in speech.
They add extra information about the tree.
checks.why: The words between the dashes tell what kind of tree it is. That is extra information.

again.title: Short, long, dots
again.text:
Look at the **size** of the mark.

**Short line** = joins words.
**Long line** = big break, look here!
**Three dots** = pause or unfinished words.
again.example:
a sugar-free drink → joins **sugar** and **free**.

The prize went to — our class! → a big break before the news.

"Well..." → a thinking pause.

slides.title: Hyphens follow rules
slides.text:
Use a hyphen in a describing group **before** a noun:

a **ten-year-old** girl

But not when the words are **not** before a noun:

The girl is **ten years old**.

In a group like ten-year-old, **every** word is joined.

slides.title: Dashes for a strong break
slides.text:
A pair of dashes can hold **extra information** in the middle of a sentence.

A single dash can add a **strong ending** or an **interruption** in speech:

"Wait, I need to —" The bell rang.

slides.title: The ellipsis has two jobs
slides.text:
1. It shows **hesitation** or words that trail off.
2. In a quotation, it shows that **some words were left out**.

"The fort ... has stood for over a century."

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
When you edit for these marks:

1. Find every hyphen, dash and ellipsis.
2. Check each against the rule: Is the describing group **before** a noun? Is the break **strong**? Is a pause or a gap really needed?
3. The sentence that breaks a rule is your proof.

sentences.t: Our team made a five-minute film.
The film was five minutes long.
It showed a one hundred year-old house.

example.explain: Sentences 1 and 2 are correct. Sentence 3 is wrong: every word in the group must be joined: **one-hundred-year-old** house.

together.passage: Our school held a three-day science fair. Fatima built a solar-powered fan. Her twelve year-old brother helped her test it. The judges said it was the most useful project in the hall. Visitors lined up all afternoon to watch it spin. She hopes to make a bigger one next year.
together.hint: Check each hyphen group that comes before a noun. Is every word in the group joined?
together.good: Yes! In twelve-year-old, all three words describe the brother, so all are joined with hyphens.

sentences: Our school held a three-day science fair.
Her twelve year-old brother helped her test it.
The judges said it was the most useful project in the hall.
Visitors lined up all afternoon to watch it spin.
She hopes to make a bigger one next year.
evidence.stem: The answer was: twelve-year-old needs a second hyphen. Tap the sentence with the mistake.
evidence.wrong: This sentence is correct. Find the sentence where a describing group is only half joined.

checks.passage: The trip took six hours. It was a six hour drive to the coast. We passed farms and small towns. By sunset we reached the sea.
checks.stem: Which sentence is missing a hyphen?
options: We passed farms and small towns.
By sunset we reached the sea.
It was a six hour drive to the coast.
checks.why: In "a six-hour drive" the words describe the noun **drive**, so they need a hyphen. "took six hours" has no noun after it, so it needs none.

checks.passage: Grandmother held up the old photo. "This was taken when I was — " She stopped and smiled. "Well, a very long time ago."
checks.stem: Why does the writer use a dash after "I was"?
options: to add a list of dates
to show she breaks off her sentence
to show a quotation was shortened
checks.why: The dash shows an interruption: she stops in the middle and starts again.

checks.passage: The museum sign says: "The fort was built from mud bricks and palm trunks, and it has stood for more than a century." A student wrote: "The fort ... has stood for more than a century."
checks.stem: What does the ellipsis in the student's sentence show?
options: Some words from the sign were left out.
checks.why: Compare the two: the words about mud bricks and palm trunks are missing. The ellipsis marks that gap.

again.title: Before the noun? Hyphen.
again.text:
Point to the noun the words describe.

1. Do the words come **right before** the noun as one group? Join them all.
2. Do they come **after** a verb? No hyphen.
again.example:
a **three-day** fair (before **fair**)

The fair lasted **three days**. (no noun after it)

slides.title: Punctuation for effect
slides.text:
Writers choose hyphens, dashes and ellipses to control **how a reader reads**.

A comma gives a small pause. A **dash** gives a sharp break. An **ellipsis** gives a slow, uncertain pause.

slides.title: Dash or parentheses?
slides.text:
Both can hold extra information.

**Dashes** make the extra words stand out.
**Parentheses** make them quiet, like a side note.

The guide — who had climbed it twenty times — went first.
The guide (a local teacher) went first.

slides.title: Ellipsis in quotations
slides.text:
When you quote a source, you may cut words that are not needed. An ellipsis shows the cut.

You must not change the meaning. If the missing words change what the source said, the quotation is unfair.

proof.title: Prove it from the text
proof.text:
To explain the effect of a mark:

1. Find the mark and read the sentence aloud in your head.
2. Ask what would change with a comma or a full stop instead.
3. Name the effect: emphasis, interruption, hesitation, or a gap in a quotation.

Point to the exact sentence where the mark creates that effect.

sentences.t: By morning, the road, the bridge, and the old market were under water.
Only one building stayed dry — the school on the hill.

example.explain: The dash creates a sharp break, so the reader's attention lands on **the school on the hill**. A comma would make it feel like just another detail.

together.passage: The report on the new library began with a short quotation from the city planner. Her full words were: "The library will open in March, although the reading garden will not be finished until summer." The newspaper printed: "The library will open in March ..." Many families planned their first visit for the opening day. Some of them were disappointed when they found the garden still closed.
together.stem: What is the problem with how the newspaper used the ellipsis?
options: It shows the planner was unsure.
It should have been a hyphen.
It cuts words that change the meaning.
It adds words the planner never said.
together.hint: Compare the full words with the printed words. What did readers not learn?
together.good: Yes! The cut words said the garden would not be ready. Without them, readers got the wrong idea.

sentences: The report on the new library began with a short quotation from the city planner.
Her full words were: "The library will open in March, although the reading garden will not be finished until summer."
The newspaper printed: "The library will open in March ..."
Many families planned their first visit for the opening day.
Some of them were disappointed when they found the garden still closed.
evidence.stem: The answer was: the ellipsis cut words that changed the meaning. Tap 2 sentences that prove it.
evidence.wrong: This sentence does not show what was cut. Compare the planner's full words with what was printed.

checks.passage: The desert seemed empty. Then, as the sun went down, the sand came alive — foxes, beetles, and tiny jumping mice.
checks.stem: What is the effect of the dash?
options: It makes the list of animals stand out as a surprise.
It shows that words were left out.
It joins two words into one adjective.
It shows the writer is unsure.
checks.why: The sharp break after "came alive" makes the reader stop, then notice the surprise list of animals.

checks.passage: Faisal looked at the last question on the test. He knew the answer yesterday. He was sure he did. "The capital of ... the capital of ..." he whispered.
checks.stem: Why does the writer use ellipses in Faisal's words?
options: to show words from a book were cut
to show his mind going blank
checks.why: The repeated, broken words and the pauses show Faisal hesitating as he tries to remember.

checks.passage: Writer A: The new bridge (which took four years to build) opened on Sunday. Writer B: The new bridge — which took four years to build — opened on Sunday.
checks.stem: How is Writer B's sentence different in effect?
options: It shows a quotation was shortened.
It hides the building time as a quiet side note.
It makes the bridge sound smaller.
It makes the four years stand out more.
checks.why: Dashes call attention to the words between them; parentheses make them sound like a quiet side note.

again.title: Swap and listen
again.text:
Replace the mark with a **comma** and read it again.

If the sentence suddenly feels flat, the mark was adding **emphasis**. If the gap disappears, it was showing **hesitation** or **cut words**.
again.example:
We opened the door — nothing.
We opened the door, nothing.

The dash makes the empty room feel sudden. The comma does not.
